en: *ṇeraṇau yatkarma ṇau cetsa kartānādhyāne* (Pāṇini 1.3.67). 1) Regarding the prescription of the *ātmanepada* endings for *ṇi*-affixes, there is the requirement that the object of the non-*ṇi*-ending verb must be perceived as the agent in that same context; otherwise, there would be over-extension (*sarvaprasaṅga*). [Mahābhāṣya: "In the prescription of *ātmanepada* for *ṇi*-affixes, it should be stated: 'When that which was the object of the non-*ṇi*-ending verb becomes the agent in the *ṇi*-ending form, then the *ātmanepada* occurs'; otherwise, there would be over-extension, and it would apply even here: *ārohanti hastinaṃ hastipakāḥ* (the elephant-keepers mount the elephant), *ārohayamāṇo hastī sthalamārohayati manuṣyān* (the elephant, being mounted, causes men to mount the dry land)."

(Kaiyaṭa: The composition of this Vārttika is because the exclusion of another object (*karmāntara*) cannot be obtained within a single sentence. For if there were syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*), the meaning would be as follows: "The *ātmanepada* occurs after a root with the causative suffix (*ṇi*) when that which was the object in the non-causative state (*aṇyantāvasthā*) becomes the agent in the causative state (*ṇyantāvasthā*), provided it is other than meditation (*ādhyāna*). This [meaning] holds true even when another object exists, as long as that which was the object in the non-causative state becomes the agent in the causative state.

2) [MaBhā] "In that case, should it be stated? It need not be stated. I shall state it thus: 'After the suffix *ṇi*, the *ātmanepada* endings occur. Then: 'if that which was the object in the non-causative (*aṇau*) is indeed the object in the causative (*ṇau*)'; then 'that is the agent, provided that it is the agent.'"

The Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*), however, establishes this meaning by relying on a division of sentences (*vākya-bheda*): "The *ātmanepada* suffix occurs after [a root] ending in *ṇi*" is one sentence; then, "if that which was the object in the *aṇi* [form] is [the agent] in the *ṇi* [form]" is the second. In this sentence, because of the necessary connection between *yat* and *tat*, the word *tat* is implied by the word *yat*. And since no other property is specified, it is the state of being an object (*karmatva*) itself that is referred back by proximity.

By the counter-indication, "Whatever is the object in the *aṇ* [causal] sense, if it is that same object in the *ṇi* [causal] sense," the exclusion of another object is effected; however, it is not established that the object of the *aṇ* retains its status as an object in the *ṇi*, because its status as an agent is established by the separate rule "if there is an agent" (*sakartṛ*), since it is contradictory for one and the same thing to simultaneously possess both the status of object and agent with respect to a single action.

By supplying the remainder of the sentence as desired—namely, "if that which is the object in the *aṇ* [causal base] is the same as the object in the *ṇi* [causative base]"—the exclusion of any other object is obtained through the implicit addition (*adhyāhāra*) of the particle *eva*. Then follows the third sentence: "it becomes the agent" (*sakartṛ*). This is intended to establish that what was the object in the *aṇ* becomes the agent in the *ṇi*. Thus, when these sentences form a single syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*), they constitute a great sentence (*mahāvākya*) that effects the grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the target form.
3) [Mahābhāṣya]: "If this is so, then this is a 'self-acting object' (*karmakartṛ*); in that case, it is established by virtue of being a self-acting object."

(Kaiyaṭa: "If it is so," [it means as follows]. Just as in the case of *lunāti kedāraṃ devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta mows the field") and *lūyate kedāraḥ svayameva* ("the field mows itself"), where the field is the *karmakartṛ* (object-agent), so too it occurs in the causative (*ṇyanta*) form: *lāvayate kedāraḥ svayameva* ("the field causes itself to be mown"). If one asks how this is so, it is explained: the root *lū* signifies both the act of causing to become two and the state of becoming two as a subordinate element—namely, *lunāti kedāraṃ devadattaḥ*, which means "Devadatta causes that [field] which is becoming two to become two."

However, when there is a desire to express the extreme ease with which the field is split, and the activity of Devadatta is not intended to be expressed, then the root *lū* (to cut) applies to the mere act of being split into two parts, since roots have multiple meanings. Roots that have different meanings are indeed distinct; their identity is only determined on account of their formal similarity. In that case, regarding the field as the agent in the process of being split into two, the operations of the object are extended [to it] by the rule "one whose action is equal to that of the object [is treated like the object]. Consequently, such usages as "the field is cut by itself" (*lūyate kedāraḥ svayameva*) are justified.

In this case as well, when the word *svayam* has the meaning "by oneself" (*ātmanā*), then since there is indeed the status of object (*karmatva*) in relation to the self, the example "the field is being reaped" (*lūyate kedāraḥ*) should be cited. However, for the authors of the Vṛtti, the mention of the word *svayam* should be understood as intended to exclude another agent. Alternatively, by the word *svayam*, the instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) of the self is established, but not its agency (*kartṛtva*).

Therefore, when the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is applied to the root *lū* (to cut), which primarily denotes the act of becoming divided into two parts, as in the case of Devadatta’s activity, then the meaning of "Devadatta cuts the field" is identical to that of "Devadatta causes the field to be cut. Furthermore, when there is a desire to express an extreme ease on the part of the field, the operation of Devadatta and others is no longer intended to be expressed, and the verb *lāvayati* comes to denote merely the act of becoming divided into two parts.

Consequently, the very same meaning as "the field cuts itself" is the same meaning as "the field causes itself to be cut. Nor does the cessation of the relationship between the prompted and the prompter entail the cessation of the *ṇic* suffix; for even when the means (*upāya*) ceases, that which is to be attained (*upeya*) does not cease. Indeed, the conceptual division of base and suffix is resorted to for the sake of deriving established words, and thus the adoption and abandonment of meanings are carried out.

In worldly usage, however, when there is a desire to express mere facility, one employs the form "lāvayate kedāraḥ" (the field causes itself to be harvested). Thus, the agent-as-object (*karmakartṛ*) has been explained by relying on this position: "The causative suffix (*ṇic*) is applied to a verbal root in its primary sense [after the causative function] has ceased."

Another alternative [for the formation of the causative] is as follows: in the sentence "Devadatta reaps the field" (*lunāti kedāraṃ devadattaḥ*), because of an excess of facility (*saukaryātiśaya*), the field (*kedāra*) prompts Devadatta who is reaping; thus, the causative suffix *ṇic* arises with respect to the activity of the field, resulting in "The field causes Devadatta to reap" (*lāvayati kedāro devadattena*). Then, when there is no intention to express the relationship between the prompted and the prompter (*prayojya-prayojaka-bhāva*), it is employed as "The field reaps by itself" (*lāvayate kedāraḥ svayameva*). In this case, by resorting to the previous grammatical analysis, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is established by the rule "like the object, [the subject behaves] as an object" (*karmavat karmaṇā*).

For instance: in the sentence "Devadatta causes the field to be harvested" (*lāvayati kedāraṃ devadattaḥ*), whatever action characterized by the field’s being split in two exists in the state of an object (*karman*) within that causative suffix (*ṇic*), that very same action exists in the state of an agent (*kartṛ*) within that same verbal root; thus, the form "the field harvests itself" (*lāvayate kedāraḥ svayameva*) is established.

However, the second method [of analysis] is shown to be possible only when this particular rule (*sūtra*) is commenced. But under that [second] method, the status of being "like the object" (*karmavadbhāva*) does not apply, because the field lacks the status of an object while the causative suffix *lāvayati* is present, and thus there is no equality of action with respect to the object within the same verbal root.

4) [Ma.bhā] "If it is argued that [the desired form] is established because of the status of being both object and agent (*karmakartṛtva*), [we reply: this statement is for the purpose of excluding *yak* and *ciṇ*. If it is argued that it is established because of the status of being both object and agent, then this must be stated for the purpose of excluding *yak* and *ciṇ*; [that is,] so that *yak* and *ciṇ*, which are prescribed when there is an object (*karman*), do not occur. (Kaiyaṭa) "For the purpose of excluding *yak* and *ciṇ*" means: this is for the sake of a restrictive rule (*niyama*) stating that if that which was the object in the *aṇ* [denominative base] becomes the agent in the *ṇi*-derived [causative], then only the *ātmanepada* suffixes are used after the *ṇi*, and no others.

5) [Mahābhāṣya] Or rather, not so; because of the prohibition of *yak* and *ciṇ*. This fault does not arise. Why? Because of the prohibition of *yak* and *ciṇ*. For here, *yak* and *ciṇ* are prohibited by the rule: "In the prohibition of *yak* and *ciṇ*, there is an addition for causative (*hetu-ṇic*), *śri*, and *brū*. (This is not found in Kaiyaṭa). 6) [Mahābhāṣya] In that case, this must be stated for the sake of those forms where the causative suffix is not used in a causal sense (*ahetumaṇic*): "Let *yak* and *ciṇ*, which are prescribed after an object (*karman*), not occur there," as in: "The tail wagged itself" (*udapupucchata pucchaṃ svayameva*).

( Kaiyaṭa: "He caused the tail to be raised" (*udapupucchata puccham*). But how can there be an object (*karman*) here for a root that does not end in *ṇic*, given that the word *puccha* denotes a substance (*dravyavacana*)? To this they reply: "In this context, the word *puccha* refers to the act of raising (*udasana-kriyā*) which has the tail as its object; therefore, the suffix *ṇiṅ* is applied in its own sense (*svārthe*)."

Therefore, when the tail, while being caused to whirl by the force of a *saṃskāra*, is intended to be expressed as acting independently during the act of whirling—just like a wheel—the rule is formulated so that the form *udapupucchata* may occur with the *ātmanepada* ending from the causative (*ṇiṅ*) stem.

In this case as well, one must proceed according to the reading of the followers of Bhāradvāja, namely, by means of a prohibition: "There should be an addition [to the prohibition] regarding the causatives (*ṇi*), *śranthi*, *granthi*, and *brū*, which are *ātmanepada*-forming and intransitive, when there is a prohibition of *yak* and *ciṇ*. (This is not found in Kaiyaṭa).

[MaBhā] And that prohibition must necessarily be resorted to—otherwise, since "where there is a restriction, there is a prohibition elsewhere," if this were not stated, one would have to state a prohibition of *yak* and *ciṇ* elsewhere than where the restriction applies, as in: "the cowherd counts the herd" (*gaṇayati gaṇaṃ gopālakaḥ*) and "the herd itself counts" (*gaṇayati gaṇaḥ svayameva*).

Regarding the statement "the *gaṇa* [root] counts the *gaṇa*": since the *gaṇa* is both the object and the agent, this rule [of *karmavat-bhāva*] does not apply there; therefore, the prohibition stated in the rule "ṇi-śranthi... must indeed be mentioned. Because that [prohibition] is all-encompassing, there is no purpose for this present rule—this is the meaning. But how, then, is the status of *karmavat-bhāva* attained here, given that *karmavat-bhāva* is prescribed only for roots whose action resides in the object (*karmastha-bhāvaka*) or whose action resides in the object (*karmastha-kriyā*)?

And *gaṇanam* (counting) is a specific type of knowledge consisting of a determination based on the cause of number; it resides in the agent. This is not a fault. The root *gaṇi* functions in the sense of "arranging by parts. A cowherd arranges the herd (*gaṇa*) as it is being arranged part by part. In that case, because it is conducive [to the action], when there is a desire to express the agency of the herd, since the action resides in the object (*karmasthabhāvaka*), there is the application of the rule *karmavadbhāva* (the object behaves like the agent). 9) [Mahābhāṣya] Regarding the middle voice (*ātmanepada*): A prohibition regarding the middle voice must be stated, as in: "The cowherd counts the herd" (*gaṇayati gaṇaṃ gopālakaḥ*)—[where one might mistakenly think] "the herd counts itself" (*gaṇayati gaṇaḥ svayameva*).

10) [MaBhā] "For the purpose of prohibiting the middle voice (*ātmanepada*": this must be stated for the purpose of prohibiting the middle voice, as in the case of *gaṇaḥ svayam eva gaṇayati* ("the group counts by itself"). Regarding "for the purpose of prohibiting the middle voice": the meaning is that it is for the sake of ensuring that the middle voice occurs when the object of the root in *ṇic* becomes the agent of the root in *ṇic*, but so that it does not occur when the object of the root in *ṇic* is the agent of the root in *ṇic*.
11) [MaBh] The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is indeed desired here.
(This is not in Kaiyaṭa.
12) [MaBh] Is it merely desired, or does it also actually apply?

[It is] desired [by some], and it follows [from the rule]. How so? Of what does this mention of *ṇiC* in the word *aṇau* refer? It refers to that *ṇiC* before which there exists either an object (*karman*) or an agent (*kartṛ*). But in this case, there is no object or agent existing prior to this *ṇiC*.

"And not from this [rule]" means: because the suffix *ṇic* is eternal (*nitya*), and since the roots of the *curādi* class are never used alone, it is impossible for there to be an object (*karman*) in the base form (*aṇau*). Therefore, the mention of "of *ṇi*" (*ṇeḥ*) refers specifically to the causal *ṇic*. Furthermore, the prohibition "in the base form" (*aṇau*) is logically applicable to that very same [causal *ṇic*] due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*). Thus, the scope of the rule—whereby there is the status of an object (*karmatva*) in the non-causal *ṇic* and the status of an agent (*kartṛtva*) in the causal *ṇic*—is indeed present here. Consequently, how could the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) be prevented by this [rule]? This is the meaning.

[MaBhā] Objection: Then this is the purpose: "I shall state 'except when there is no mental visualization' (anādhyāne). This is so that it does not apply here: "The cuckoo remembers the forest thicket; the forest thicket itself causes him to remember."

(Kaiyaṭa: "In that case, this [sūtra]... Since a prohibition cannot be established when its scope is not specified, the entire sūtra is formulated. Regarding "of the forest-thicket" (*vanagulmasya*): this is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an elliptical indication). For here, because the forest-thicket is intended as a subordinate element (*śeṣa*), it lacks the status of an object (*karman*). Therefore, one should have demonstrated it simply as "he remembers the forest-thicket" (*smarati vanagulmam*). Regarding "he causes him to remember" (*smarayaty enam*): this too is an *upalakṣaṇa*.

For here, because of the existence of the object (*karman*) in the phrase "him [the bee]," the application of *karmavadbhāva* (the treatment as an object) does not occur, due to the rule: "Intransitives are treated like transitives. Nor does this [rule] apply to the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), because another object exists. Therefore, it should be demonstrated that "the forest thicket causes itself to be remembered" (*smarayati vanagulmaḥ svayameva*). 14) [Mahābhāṣya] This too is not a valid purpose. Rules prescribed for the object apply to those whose state (*bhāva*) resides in the object or whose action (*kriyā*) resides in the object; however, this [verb] has its state residing in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvaka*).

(Kaiyaṭa: Not present) 15) [Mahābhāṣya] Since this is already established, the fact that the Teacher teaches the prohibition "provided there is no intention" (*anādhyāne*) indicates that the Ātmanepada occurs even for such types of verbs. What is the purpose of this indication? It is so that the Ātmanepada is established in such cases as: *paśyanti bhṛtyā rājānam* ("the servants see the king") and *darśayate bhṛtyān rājā* ("the king causes the servants to see himself").

"Of those of this class," [it is said]. The meaning is that for those roots which are *aṇi*-ant (without the causative suffix) and have a certain object, when they are *ṇi*-ant (with the causative suffix) and that same object becomes the agent (*kartṛ*), then the *ātmanepada* ending occurs even though the action resides in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvakriyatva*). By stating this, the author of the Bhāṣya indicates that this rule is prescriptive (*vidhyartha*). Consequently, in examples such as "the elephant makes itself mount" (*ārohayate hastī*), the *ātmanepada* is established by this very rule.

For instance—the author of the Bhāṣya will state under *ruhiḥ gativiśeṣavacanaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.36) that "in the Vedic language, [the suffix] hitu follows a root when it signifies a specific kind of motion. Thus, because the action resides in the agent (*kartṛsthakriyatva*), there is no application of the rule for treating the verb as if it had an object (*karmavadbhāva*). Consequently, those who demonstrate the application of *karmavadbhāva* in such cases as "the elephant mounts by itself" (*āruhyate hastī svayam eva*) are to be disregarded, as they contradict both logic and the Bhāṣya. For it has been said: "The determination of the action resides in that where a specific change is observed; however, for others, the determination of the action is established solely by means of words."

The location of the action is stated either by means of perceiving its specific qualities or by following the verbal designation. And these two reasons establish that the act of ascending resides in the agent (*kartṛsthatā*), not in the object (*karmasthatā*). For instance, in expressions such as "he ascends an elephant," "he ascends a tree," or "he ascends a mountain," no difference in the form of the act of ascending is perceived despite the difference in the objects.

Furthermore, no distinction produced by action (*kriyā*) is observed among these grammatical applications (*prayoga*s). By means of the verbal root (*dhātu*), it is the action residing in the agent (*kartṛ*) that is expressed, not the action residing in the object (*karman*). It is merely because the object is a *kāraka* (participant in the action) that an action must necessarily exist; thus, the action is inferred. For all *kāraka*s perform their respective individual operations and bring about the principal action. This matter is indeed extensive, but it has been stated here only as it is relevant to the present topic.

Let us return to the subject at hand: "The king causes his servants to see [himself]. Now, one might object: since there is another action present here, the ātmanepada suffix should not occur. It is replied: from this very example, the intention of the authors of the Bhāṣya is inferred.

"In the presence of another object distinct from those that were the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*) in the state prior to the causative suffix (*aṇ*), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) does not occur; for example, in *sthalam ārohayati manuṣyān* ('he causes men to ascend the dry land'). However, in the present case, since the servants—who were the agents in the non-causative state—become the objects under the causative suffix (*ṇau*), the middle voice indeed occurs. Thus, even though the cuckoo is the object in *smarayaty enaṃ vanagulmaḥ* ('the forest thicket causes him to remember'), it is appropriate as a counter-example."

16) [Mahābhāṣya] Prohibition regarding the self as the object. A prohibition must be stated regarding the self as the object, as in: "He kills himself" (*hanty ātmānam*) or "He causes himself to be killed" (*ghātayaty ātmā*).

Regarding the phrase "regarding the self as the object": the meaning is that when a single entity is mentally divided and intended to be expressed both as the object and as the agent, then the prohibition applies.
17) That [prohibition], then, must be stated.

Or rather, it need not be stated, because in the case of a causative (*ṇyanta*), there is a different agent. Why? Because in the causative, there is a different agent. Here, that which is the object in the non-causative form is one thing, while the agent of the causative is another. How so? There are two selves: the inner self (*antarātman*) and the bodily self (*śarīrātman*). The inner self performs that action by which the bodily self experiences pleasure and pain; the bodily self performs that action by which the inner self experiences pleasure and pain.

(Kaiyaṭa: "Not indeed" means that in reality there is a distinction between the self [as agent and object], and not that a single entity can simultaneously possess the status of both object and agent. Regarding "the inner self": in the Sāṃkhya view, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is the inner self, because agency is possible for it alone. However, in the view of the Naiyāyikas, since the Spirit (*puruṣa*) possesses agency, it is that very Spirit which is intended here as the inner self. Regarding "the body-self experiences pleasure and pain": it should be explained that because the body is insentient, it is the body that becomes connected with the causes of pleasure and pain.
